guests.name: Richard Feynman
guests.story: Feynman’s account of quantum electrodynamics shows several routes toward one calculation. His scientific-integrity argument also underlies your public Mongla measurement ledger.

quotes.context: The warning includes the experimenter: evidence against a favorite idea belongs in the report too.
quotes.question: Which result would make us change our mind?

quotes.text: We must publish both kinds of result.
quotes.context: A disappointing measurement still tells the next engineer something useful.
quotes.question: Would we keep this result if it looked less impressive?

quotes.context: He asks experimenters to disclose weaknesses rather than present only the convincing half of a result.
quotes.question: What uncertainty have we left out of the graph?

quotes.context: Scientific integrity demands more than technically truthful individual statements.
quotes.question: Could the presentation imply more than we measured?

quotes.text: Science is the belief in the ignorance of experts.
quotes.context: Expertise can guide a test; it cannot replace checking the claim.
quotes.question: What would we measure rather than accept on authority?

quotes.text: what we know and what we call it
quotes.context: His father distinguished naming inertia from explaining an observation.
quotes.question: Can I explain the mechanism without using its name?

quotes.context: His account treats questioning inherited explanations as part of scientific practice.
quotes.question: Which familiar explanation should we test for ourselves?

quotes.context: In his Nobel lecture, mathematical proposals still need consistency and contact with physical results.
quotes.question: What constraints must our proposed equation satisfy?

quotes.context: Different formulations can suggest different paths into an unsolved problem.
quotes.question: Can we represent this problem in another way?

quotes.context: He distinguishes a useful formulation from a claim that it is the only possible route.
quotes.question: Are we mistaking our preferred method for a requirement?

quotes.text: reality must take precedence over public relations
quotes.context: The claim is answerable to component evidence and actual operating conditions, not a comforting public message.
quotes.question: Which reliability claim in our work needs better evidence?

topics.title: Names are not mechanisms
topics.story: His bird example separates knowing a name from investigating behavior.
topics.task: Describe one sensor's behavior without using its technical name.
topics.question: What does the name hide from us?

topics.title: The feather question
topics.story: A walk with his father becomes an investigation of what a bird is actually doing.
topics.task: Observe one ordinary object for five minutes before searching for an explanation.
topics.question: What did we notice before we looked it up?

topics.title: Honest negative results
topics.story: His integrity argument includes reporting results that do not support the preferred conclusion.
topics.task: Keep a failed calibration beside the successful one with its conditions intact.
topics.question: What would disappear if we only saved the pretty plot?

topics.title: The experimenter is vulnerable
topics.story: Self-deception is part of the experimental problem, not merely someone else's flaw.
topics.task: Write the outcome you hope for, then design a test that could reject it.
topics.question: Which measurement would disappoint us usefully?

topics.title: The missing control
topics.story: The Young rat experiment in his address examines overlooked experimental cues.
topics.task: Change one nuisance cue in an experiment while preserving the intended signal.
topics.question: Are we measuring our hypothesis or a hidden shortcut?

topics.title: Replication has conditions
topics.story: He distinguishes a convincing-looking procedure from understanding what actually makes it work.
topics.task: List the conditions another person needs to reproduce your measurement.
topics.question: Could someone repeat this without borrowing our assumptions?

topics.title: Many routes, one prediction
topics.story: His Nobel lecture recounts different approaches to the same quantum-electrodynamics calculations.
topics.task: Derive a small result in two independent ways and compare the boundary cases.
topics.question: Do the two routes agree for the same reason?

topics.title: An unfinished idea is evidence
topics.story: The lecture describes the development of ideas rather than presenting a frictionless discovery story.
topics.task: Save an abandoned derivation with the exact step that stopped working.
topics.question: Can a failed route teach the next attempt something?

topics.title: Small particles, large consequences
topics.story: The first physics lecture uses the atomic picture to connect everyday properties with microscopic motion.
topics.task: Sketch how a temperature change could alter a material measurement.
topics.question: Which microscopic change could explain the macroscopic effect?

topics.title: Analogy has a boundary
topics.story: The quantum-behavior chapter compares bullets, water waves and electrons before exposing the limits of those comparisons.
topics.task: Compare two models of one observation and name where each analogy fails.
topics.question: Which familiar picture has quietly stopped being valid?

topics.title: Reliability is not a public-relations number
topics.story: His Challenger appendix contrasts management confidence with engineers' estimates, examines component evidence and argues against treating an absence of failures as proof of adequate margin.
topics.task: Write a reliability claim with its evidence, uncertainty and operating conditions; do not substitute a reassuring number.
topics.question: What evidence supports this margin when the environment changes?

guests.name: John Carmack
guests.story: Carmack’s engineering writing examines latency, state and execution order. The useful Den connection is concrete: trace the work a frame actually performs before adding another abstraction.

quotes.context: Low latency depends on several stages cooperating, not only one fast function.
quotes.question: Where does the oldest input spend its time?

quotes.context: Queued frames can preserve throughput while increasing the delay a person feels.
quotes.question: Did we measure latency as well as frame rate?

quotes.context: His discussion explores correcting a displayed view using newer motion information.
quotes.question: Which part of our result could use a fresher measurement?

quotes.context: When operations are inherently ordered, their execution order should be visible.
quotes.question: Can we trace the whole path without guessing which call runs next?

quotes.context: For a single-use function, he considers whether an extra boundary is actually helping.
quotes.question: What does this helper clarify, and what does it hide?

quotes.text: try to make it completely functional.
quotes.context: A nearly pure computation may become easier to reason about by exposing its remaining dependencies.
quotes.question: Which hidden state can become an explicit input?

quotes.text: code duplication is a greater evil
quotes.context: His argument for visible execution is not a license to copy logic everywhere.
quotes.question: Can we preserve one implementation and still make the ordering clear?

quotes.context: Even when hardware has side effects, a useful programming abstraction can make reasoning clearer.
quotes.question: At which boundary is this model useful, and where does it stop?

quotes.text: Pure functions have a lot of nice properties.
quotes.context: Explicit inputs and outputs make testing and reuse easier to inspect.
quotes.question: Could we test this calculation without starting the entire application?

quotes.context: The quoted claim concerns pure functions with value parameters, not arbitrary shared mutable objects.
quotes.question: Are all the inputs really values, or is something shared underneath?

quotes.context: His retrospective points to reusing a representation already serving another part of the engine.
quotes.question: Which second implementation could our existing representation replace?

topics.title: Latency is a chain
topics.story: His latency discussion follows delays across multiple cooperating parts of an interactive system.
topics.task: Measure input-to-visible-response delay and draw the full path.
topics.question: Which delay did we accidentally omit from the total?

topics.title: Prediction can be wrong
topics.story: Latency mitigation includes prediction and the consequences when a predicted state differs from reality.
topics.task: Compare an extrapolated sensor state with a later ground-truth measurement.
topics.question: How does this feel when the prediction fails?

topics.title: Local clarity, global behavior
topics.story: His inlining discussion considers code visibility and the difficulty of reasoning across calls.
topics.task: Read a critical path as one continuous sequence before extracting abstractions.
topics.question: What important state change was hidden behind a tidy function name?

topics.title: Repeated code has a cost too
topics.story: The archived exchange weighs the consequences of organization choices rather than treating one style as universally correct.
topics.task: Compare duplication and extraction for one real maintenance change.
topics.question: Which arrangement makes the next bug easier to see?

topics.title: Pure computations are inspectable
topics.story: His functional-programming essay distinguishes useful purity from unrelated language conveniences.
topics.task: Extract one calculation so inputs determine outputs without hidden mutation.
topics.question: Could this result change while its apparent inputs stay the same?

topics.title: State needs a border
topics.story: The essay examines the practical value of controlling side effects in an imperative codebase.
topics.task: Draw the boundary between a pure calculation and its device or file access.
topics.question: Where does the outside world enter this function?

topics.title: A language label is not the benefit
topics.story: He separates pure-function benefits from syntax, libraries and other features often grouped under functional programming.
topics.task: Name the exact property you want before adopting a programming style.
topics.question: Are we improving a property or collecting a label?

topics.title: The frame is a deadline
topics.story: Interactive latency makes timing visible to the person using the system.
topics.task: Set a response-time budget for a real UI or control interaction and measure it.
topics.question: What part of the budget belongs to us?

topics.title: Correctness before elegance
topics.story: The correspondence treats code structure as an engineering tradeoff with practical failure modes.
topics.task: Take an elegant refactor and prove one important behavior stayed unchanged.
topics.question: Which invariant deserves a test before we admire the code?

topics.title: Make effects explicit
topics.story: His practical discussion asks how functional ideas help actual C++ programs.
topics.task: Replace one implicit shared-state dependency with an explicit argument.
topics.question: What dependency could a reviewer now see immediately?

topics.title: The simpler solution already had a home
topics.story: In the DOOM source-release notes, he looks back at messy movement and sight tests and observes that the BSP tree already used for rendering could have supported a simpler solution. A shipped achievement still contained things he would improve.
topics.task: Find a representation already present in your project that could remove a second, fragile implementation.
topics.question: Have we already built the thing that could simplify this?

guests.name: Andrej Karpathy
guests.story: Karpathy’s training recipe starts with data inspection and simple baselines. His recurrent-network essay makes stateful computation tangible with small implementations and inspected outputs.

quotes.context: Inspect examples and distributions before assuming that a training failure belongs to the model.
quotes.question: What does an actual difficult sample look like?

quotes.context: Fitting a tiny batch checks whether the training pipeline can learn at all.
quotes.question: Can our model deliberately memorize two examples?

quotes.context: The input tensor immediately before inference is more trustworthy than an earlier preview.
quotes.question: Have we looked at exactly what the model receives?

quotes.context: A running training loop can produce plausible numbers while containing a serious mistake.
quotes.question: What test could fail even if the loss decreases?

quotes.context: An expected initial loss is a useful inexpensive sanity check.
quotes.question: What loss should an untrained model produce here?

quotes.context: Controlling randomness helps distinguish a code change from a different experimental draw.
quotes.question: Which variables did we change besides the code?

quotes.context: A recurrent network can be viewed as a repeated state transition rather than a mysterious box.
quotes.question: What state changes at one step?

quotes.context: A small input/output interface can conceal dependence on an entire preceding sequence.
quotes.question: What history is hiding behind this interface?

quotes.context: The learned computation carries information forward across steps.
quotes.question: Can we trace a three-step example by hand?

quotes.context: His simplest RNN example makes the persistent state explicit.
quotes.question: What information could fit in this state, and what would be lost?

quotes.text: Our policy network is a 2-layer fully-connected net.
quotes.context: A small visible mechanism makes the learning loop approachable; the historical example is not a claim about the latest RL frontier.
quotes.question: Can we trace one rewarded action all the way to a parameter update?

topics.title: Look at actual data
topics.story: His training recipe begins with careful inspection of the dataset before complicated modeling.
topics.task: View ten raw examples with their labels and record something surprising.
topics.question: What did a real example tell us that the aggregate hid?

topics.title: Tiny-data overfitting
topics.story: The recipe uses overfitting a small batch as a debugging check.
topics.task: Make a tiny model fit a tiny trusted subset before scaling the run.
topics.question: If it cannot learn five examples, why trust fifty thousand?

topics.title: One improvement at a time
topics.story: His staged recipe adds complexity after establishing a working baseline.
topics.task: Change one training ingredient and preserve the previous baseline results.
topics.question: Which change actually earned the improvement?

topics.title: Recurrent character behavior
topics.story: His recurrent-network essay explores character-level generation and interprets observed behaviors.
topics.task: Train a deliberately small character model and inspect both good and broken outputs.
topics.question: What pattern did it learn, and what did we imagine it learned?

topics.title: A scalar autograd engine
topics.story: Micrograd exposes reverse-mode differentiation through a compact scalar engine.
topics.task: Differentiate a two-input expression by hand and compare every stored gradient.
topics.question: Can we point to the exact multiplication that moved this gradient?

topics.title: Gradient checks are witnesses
topics.story: The repository includes tests comparing gradients against PyTorch.
topics.task: Compare an analytic gradient with a finite-difference approximation on a tiny case.
topics.question: Does agreement survive a changed input?

topics.title: Start with counts
topics.story: Makemore presents several character-model families, including a simple bigram model.
topics.task: Build a count-based baseline before training a more expressive name generator.
topics.question: How much structure did the simplest model already capture?

topics.title: Architectures can be compared
topics.story: The project places multiple model families around the same character-generation task.
topics.task: Compare two models on the same split and inspect their characteristic failures.
topics.question: Did capacity help the task or only flatter the training set?

topics.title: A training loop without magic
topics.story: Llm.c makes language-model training visible in C and CUDA.
topics.task: Follow one forward pass, loss, backward pass and parameter update through the implementation.
topics.question: Where did a tensor become bytes in a buffer?

topics.title: Reference behavior matters
topics.story: The project includes correctness and performance comparisons alongside the training implementation.
topics.task: Keep a trusted reference output while optimizing one small kernel.
topics.question: Did the faster answer remain the same answer?

topics.title: Pong is not magic in a box
topics.story: His Pong tutorial follows a two-layer policy network from pixels and sampled actions to a policy-gradient update. It makes a working learning loop inspectable rather than relying on the impressive appearance of a game-playing agent.
topics.task: Trace one action, its eventual reward and the update that changes that action's probability.
topics.question: Where exactly did the reward turn into a change in behavior?

guests.name: Chris Lattner
guests.story: Lattner describes LLVM as reusable compiler libraries. His later Mojo discussions connect language design, existing ecosystems and hardware capability instead of treating them as separate concerns.

quotes.context: LLVM’s early architecture sought components that could serve different languages and targets.
quotes.question: What can another project reuse without copying our whole application?

quotes.context: Passes can evolve more independently when their boundaries do not require knowledge of every other pass.
quotes.question: Which assumption couples these two modules unnecessarily?

quotes.context: Some limitations come from a system’s structure rather than a local inefficient operation.
quotes.question: Are we tuning a function or repairing a boundary?

quotes.text: LLVM doesn't magically solve all optimization problems!
quotes.context: A modular architecture creates opportunities; it does not remove the need to understand the optimization.
quotes.question: Which part still requires measurement and domain knowledge?

quotes.context: Reusing a familiar language surface can reduce the cost of adopting a new implementation model.
quotes.question: What should stay familiar while the internals improve?

quotes.context: The interview presents building a language as a deliberate cost-benefit decision, not an automatic virtue.
quotes.question: What benefit would justify this new maintenance burden?

quotes.text: Programmers I've seen generally love growing
quotes.context: An effective tool can help people acquire capabilities without discarding what they already know.
quotes.question: Does this interface help us learn one useful new idea?

quotes.context: Putting capabilities in libraries can keep the language boundary smaller and more adaptable.
quotes.question: Does this need new syntax, or would a library be enough?

quotes.text: this complexity is really slowing everything down.
quotes.context: A short excerpt on the design tradeoff: verify the surrounding interview before treating simplicity as a universal rule.
quotes.question: Which complexity are we moving, rather than removing?

quotes.text: most people don’t wanna know about the compiler.
quotes.context: His compiler work ties language choices to the behavior of the generated program.
quotes.question: Can we show where the speedup comes from?

quotes.text: The LLVM virtual instruction set is the glue that holds the system together.
quotes.context: The representation connects optimization stages; an interface becomes useful because it preserves what those stages need.
quotes.question: What meaning has to survive our next interface boundary?

topics.title: Three compiler responsibilities
topics.story: The LLVM chapter separates frontend, optimizer and backend responsibilities.
topics.task: Trace one expression through parsing, representation, transformation and code generation.
topics.question: Which layer owns the meaning we are changing?

topics.title: An IR is a shared language
topics.story: A common intermediate representation enables reuse between different language and target paths.
topics.task: Represent one tiny program in a form two independent tools can inspect.
topics.question: What agreement lets these tools cooperate?

topics.title: A pass should have a contract
topics.story: The chapter explains modular optimization passes and their management.
topics.task: Describe the precondition and preserved property of one transformation.
topics.question: What remains true after the clever part runs?

topics.title: Libraries instead of a lump
topics.story: The architecture makes compiler components reusable rather than forcing one monolithic tool.
topics.task: Use one component without invoking the entire application around it.
topics.question: Which interface made selective reuse possible?

topics.title: Diagnostics are part of the product
topics.story: The chapter discusses Clang as a language frontend with tooling and diagnostic concerns.
topics.task: Rewrite one error so the next person knows what to inspect or change.
topics.question: Does this message explain a cause or merely announce disappointment?

topics.title: Runtime specialization
topics.story: LLVM is described in uses beyond ahead-of-time compilation, including runtime specialization.
topics.task: Compare a general implementation with a version specialized for one known input property.
topics.question: Which fact became available only at runtime?

topics.title: Language design is collaborative
topics.story: His Swift account credits language specialists, documentation work and internal dogfooding.
topics.task: Ask a real user to try one language or API change before polishing it.
topics.question: Which assumption did ordinary use break first?

topics.title: Interoperability is a constraint
topics.story: The Mojo discussion considers high-performance programming alongside existing developer ecosystems.
topics.task: Define what must remain compatible before improving a system boundary.
topics.question: What useful thing would a clean rewrite accidentally strand?

topics.title: Different levels need different tools
topics.story: The interview spans compiler infrastructure, language design and AI-oriented systems.
topics.task: Choose the abstraction level at which one bug can actually be observed.
topics.question: Are we debugging the problem or the layer we like best?

topics.title: Modularity needs meaning
topics.story: The chapter's reusable components depend on representations and explicit responsibilities.
topics.task: Remove one dependency from a component and check whether its contract still makes sense.
topics.question: Did we make a module or just another folder?

topics.title: A thesis about the glue
topics.story: His master's thesis presents LLVM as infrastructure for optimization at several stages. The intermediate representation connects those stages; the architecture is more than one clever optimization pass.
topics.task: Draw the representation that lets two stages of your pipeline cooperate without sharing every implementation detail.
topics.question: What information must survive the boundary for the next stage to reason correctly?

guests.name: Paul Graham
guests.story: Graham’s essays connect useful ideas with observed needs and protect the uninterrupted time needed to build them. His startup advice is context, not a universal instruction for every engineering project.

quotes.text: Live in the future, then build what's missing.
quotes.context: He recommends noticing gaps from direct experience rather than inventing needs in the abstract.
quotes.question: What problem did we actually encounter this week?

quotes.context: Curiosity can expose an opportunity before it looks like a business plan.
quotes.question: What would we build even without a pitch deck?

quotes.context: In this essay, attention to missing things matters more than forcing an idea on demand.
quotes.question: What inconvenience have we learned to ignore?

quotes.context: Early hands-on work can reveal what a polished automated system would otherwise conceal.
quotes.question: Which manual step would teach us something before automating it?

quotes.context: A new product may need deliberate contact with real users rather than waiting for discovery.
quotes.question: Who could try this and tell us where it breaks?

quotes.context: Care at a small scale can uncover what people value about a tool.
quotes.question: Which small improvement would make today's use noticeably easier?

quotes.context: A maker often needs a larger continuous block than a calendar’s smallest appointment slot.
quotes.question: What work needs a protected uninterrupted block?

quotes.context: The essay compares a maker’s interrupted flow with a manager’s scheduling needs.
quotes.question: Could this discussion be handled without breaking the work block?

quotes.text: learn not to lie to yourself
quotes.context: Effort alone is not a substitute for choosing worthwhile work and developing the relevant skill.
quotes.question: Are we pushing on the right part of this problem?

quotes.context: The essay’s discussion of hard work includes learning how to work effectively, not merely accumulating hours.
quotes.question: What did this attempt teach us about how we work?

quotes.context: Simplicity here is a demand on craft and problem solving, not permission to remove necessary behavior.
quotes.question: What could become simpler without becoming less useful?

topics.title: Problems before startup poses
topics.story: His startup-ideas essay looks for real unmet needs rather than merely plausible company concepts.
topics.task: Write down a problem you repeatedly experience before naming a product.
topics.question: Would we still want this fixed without the launch announcement?

topics.title: Do the unscalable thing
topics.story: He argues that manual early work can reveal what users actually need.
topics.task: Help one person complete a task manually before automating the workflow.
topics.question: Which detail would automation have hidden from us?

topics.title: Protect the maker's block
topics.story: His schedule essay distinguishes the working rhythms of makers and managers.
topics.task: Reserve one uninterrupted block for a task with expensive context loading.
topics.question: What did that tiny meeting interrupt besides its own duration?

topics.title: Effort needs direction
topics.story: The essay examines hard work together with ability and genuine interest.
topics.task: Compare a week of effort with the specific skill or result it improved.
topics.question: Were we working hard on the right difficulty?

topics.title: The frontier has gaps
topics.story: His great-work essay describes learning enough to notice overlooked gaps.
topics.task: Find one small unanswered question in a topic you already know reasonably well.
topics.question: What looks obvious from far away but unclear up close?

topics.title: Curiosity can steer
topics.story: The essay treats curiosity as a guide to choosing and exploring work.
topics.task: Follow one unusually persistent question long enough to produce a small artifact.
topics.question: Which question keeps returning when nobody assigns it?

topics.title: Early work can look awkward
topics.story: He writes about the difficulty of judging unfinished early work by mature standards.
topics.task: Keep a rough first version long enough to learn what it could become.
topics.question: Are we judging a seed by the shade it does not yet cast?

topics.title: Solve your own recurring pain
topics.story: The essay connects noticing problems with direct familiarity rather than detached brainstorming.
topics.task: Keep a short log of friction in your real robotics or development day.
topics.question: Which annoyance has earned a prototype through repetition?

topics.title: Delight is concrete work
topics.story: His early-company advice includes unusually attentive service rather than abstract user enthusiasm.
topics.task: Improve one frustrating step for one real user and watch them try it.
topics.question: What changed for the person rather than for our pitch?

topics.title: Ambition still needs a next step
topics.story: The essay connects large ambitions with sustained work at a field's frontier.
topics.task: Choose the smallest artifact that moves an ambitious question forward this week.
topics.question: What can we actually make before we name the revolution?

topics.title: Taste gets tested by constraints
topics.story: Taste for Makers connects simplicity across different crafts and considers how difficult constraints can force more elegant solutions. This is an argument about making good work, not a claim that all minimal-looking work is good.
topics.task: Remove one decorative or structural element and check whether the result becomes clearer, weaker or merely emptier.
topics.question: Did we simplify the experience or just delete something useful?

guests.name: Tim Urban
guests.story: Urban uses diagrams and characters to make habits and assumptions visible. His essays are useful thinking prompts; the illustrated metaphors are not clinical models of the brain.

quotes.text: The chef reasons from first principles
quotes.context: The chef metaphor asks where a rule came from rather than merely copying the recipe.
quotes.question: Which assumption can we derive instead of borrowing?

quotes.text: No one else knows shit either.
quotes.context: This provocative heading challenges automatic deference, not the value of expertise or evidence.
quotes.question: Whose conclusion are we treating as certain without checking?

quotes.text: negative feedback is a free boost
quotes.context: In the essay’s metaphor, criticism can supply information for revising a model.
quotes.question: What useful signal is hiding in this uncomfortable feedback?

quotes.context: This is his fictional character for choosing immediate ease over a longer-term intention.
quotes.question: What easy distraction is currently steering the wheel?

quotes.context: His metaphor describes leisure that feels uneasy because an intended task remains unresolved.
